group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 69-year-old man presented to the multidisciplinary pre-operative clinic eight days before a planned right reverse total shoulder arthroplasty intended to relieve progressively painful pseudoparalysis stemming from chronic rotator-cuff tear arthropathy; the orthopedic team anticipates a 90-minute deltopectoral approach under general anesthesia with an overnight stay on the usual postoperative ward for sling fitting and early pendulum exercises. He arrived alone, parked on the third deck of the hospital garage, and walked the 100-meter distance to registration without pausing, conversing easily while removing his jacket; he reports that he still mows his small lawn with a self-propelled mower, carries groceries up one flight of stairs, and completes a 30-minute indoor cycling session on most evenings, limiting use of the injured arm because of pain rather than breathlessness or fatigue. He sleeps flat, has not awakened acutely short of breath, has not noticed ankle swelling, and last recorded his home weight at 186 lb, unchanged for the past year. Six years ago he developed sudden slurred speech and transient clumsiness of his left hand while reading the newspaper; brain MRI demonstrated a small right internal capsule lacunar infarction without hemorrhage, and symptoms resolved completely over a subsequent week of inpatient rehabilitation. He remains adherent to daily aspirin 81 mg and high-intensity atorvastatin started at discharge and has had no recurrent focal neurologic events, vision changes, or gait imbalance; annual neurologic follow-ups remain stable, and carotid ultrasonography last winter showed non-flow-limiting bilateral plaques. Type 2 diabetes mellitus was diagnosed 18 years ago; oral agents sufficed for a decade, but progressive fasting hyperglycemia led to initiation of basal insulin four years ago. He currently injects insulin glargine 26 units each night and uses insulin lispro before meals following a 1:12 carbohydrate ratio with a correction factor of 1 unit for every 30 mg/dL above 150. Continuous glucose monitor downloads reviewed by his endocrinologist three weeks ago revealed 72 % time in the 70–180 mg/dL range, with no assistance-requiring hypoglycemia; most recent hemoglobin A1c was 7.8 %. Blood pressure has been well controlled with lisinopril 20 mg each morning and amlodipine 5 mg nightly, and hyperlipidemia is treated with the aforementioned statin. He denies chest tightness, exertional jaw or arm discomfort, palpitations, dizzy spells, syncope, or prior coronary testing. There is no personal history of valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, chronic lung disorder, peripheral arterial claudication, or abdominal aneurysm. Surgical history includes laparoscopic cholecystectomy at age 45 without complications and remote right inguinal hernia repair. He quit cigarette smoking 22 years ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks a 12-ounce beer with weekend dinner, and denies illicit drug use. Family history is notable for a brother who suffered an ischemic stroke at 72; no first-degree relatives experienced premature coronary events. Review of systems today is negative for fevers, cough, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, abdominal pain, melena, or unintentional weight change. After five minutes seated, vital signs recorded blood pressure 122/70 mm Hg in the right arm, regular pulse 68 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air, oral temperature 36.7 °C, and body mass index 28 kg/m². The patient appeared comfortable and euvolemic. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruit, and the point of maximal impulse was localized to the fifth intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line without displacement. Auscultation revealed crisp S1 and S2 with no gallop, click, or murmur. Lungs sounded vesicular throughout without crackles or wheezes. Abdominal examination was soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds and no hepato-splenomegaly. Extremities were warm with 2 + dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses and no edema. Neurologic screening showed full orientation, intact cranial nerves, symmetric strength except for painful limitation of right shoulder abduction, normal sensation, coordination, and a steady heel-to-toe gait. Right shoulder evaluation demonstrated pseudoparalysis beyond 30 ° of abduction, positive external rotation lag, and a well-preserved deltoid; skin was intact without prior surgical scars. Pre-operative laboratory tests drawn one hour before the visit revealed hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 7.1 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 238 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, chloride 103 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 25 mg/dL, and serum creatinine 1.58 mg/dL, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 48 mL/min/1.73 m². Fasting plasma glucose obtained simultaneously was 138 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase, alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, and international normalized ratio were within reference limits. A 12-lead electrocardiogram printed during the visit showed normal sinus rhythm at 66 beats per minute, normal intervals, axis at 30 °, and nonspecific T-wave flattening in the anterior leads unchanged from a tracing six months ago. Upright posteroanterior chest radiograph displayed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment by anesthesia documented Mallampati class II visualization, inter-incisor distance 4 cm, thyromental distance 6 cm, and full cervical extension. The anesthesia plan includes continuation of ACE inhibitor and statin the morning of surgery, withholding the evening dose of glargine to 75 % of usual, point-of-care glucose on arrival with subcutaneous corrective lispro only if greater than 180 mg/dL, standard induction with endotracheal intubation, and placement of an ultrasound-guided interscalene block for postoperative analgesia. Mechanical calf pumps and chemoprophylaxis with low-dose low-molecular-weight heparin will be initiated the night of surgery. After detailed discussion of operative approach, bleeding, nerve injury, infection, thromboembolic, metabolic, and neurologic risks, the patient demonstrated teach-back regarding medication management and fasting instructions, voiced understanding, and expressed determination to regain overhead function and return to recreational kayaking by summer.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index assigns 1 point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery (intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or suprainguinal vascular): shoulder arthroplasty is orthopedic → 0.
- History of ischemic heart disease: none documented → 0.
- History of heart failure: none documented → 0.
- Cerebrovascular disease: prior MRI-confirmed lacunar stroke counts despite complete recovery → 1.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: uses glargine and lispro → 1.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: creatinine 1.58 mg/dL → 0.
Total = 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2.
Final answer: 2
